918.title: Numbers from India
918.hook: the Indian numerals, with zero, travel west through Arabic books
918.howItsDone: Scholars writing in Arabic taught the Indian place-value system in their books, calling it Indian reckoning, and readers in Europe later learned it from those books.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Khwarizmi and algebra: a book of two fair moves for dividing an inheritance. Your line was: restoring and balancing. Where did something need restoring yesterday? Day nine hundred eighteen.

Try writing today's day number, nine hundred eighteen, in Roman numerals. You get a tangle of letters, and adding two of them together is a headache. Now write it the usual way, a handful of digits in a row, and any schoolchild can add it. The trick is in the empty places. A small circle that means nothing is here, and because it holds the place, every other digit knows what it is worth. In English those digits are often called Arabic numerals. In the Arabic books of Baghdad, the method had another name. They called it Indian reckoning.
screen: `A TANGLE OF LETTERS.` → `A ROW OF DIGITS.` → `INDIAN RECKONING.`

segments.voice: The idea came from India. Indian mathematicians wrote numbers with a small set of signs, where a sign's place in the row tells you its size. A sign on the far right counts ones. One step left, tens. Another step, hundreds. And when a place is empty, you need a mark that says so, or the whole row slides. That mark is the one we call zero. Scholars writing in Arabic took up this Indian way of counting and wrote books to teach it. Al-Khwarizmi, from yesterday, is credited with one of them. Later readers in Europe learned the method from those Arabic books, and so in Europe the figures got an Arabic name, while the Arabic books themselves kept calling them Indian. Both names are honest. Each one tells you where a neighbor first met the idea. The Arabic word for the empty place was sifr, meaning empty. So nothing became a number. An emptiness that you can write down, add, and build on. A row of digits works because some places are allowed to be empty and still be counted. The Qur'an says that God keeps count of all things, and some Muslim readers have heard in that a reason to count carefully and honestly. Whatever the reason, the empty place now had a mark of its own, and a long sum could be written down, and checked, one place at a time.
screen: `A SIGN'S PLACE TELLS ITS SIZE.` · `AN EMPTY PLACE NEEDS A MARK.` · `ARABIC BOOKS CALLED IT INDIAN.` · `SIFR: THE EMPTY ONE.` · then, large: `NOTHING, AS A NUMBER.`

segments.voice: The practice: write zero. Take any pen and paper, or trace it with a finger on your palm. Draw one slow circle. Settle, and breathe. Look at the empty middle. Breathe in. Notice that it is not nothing at all. It holds a place. Breathe out. Then let the circle stand for one empty place in your own day, a gap in the calendar or a quiet hour, and let it be counted as part of the day, not a waste. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet with God. If you don't, just rest in it. The bell holds the time.
Numbers from India. A way of counting by place, with a mark for the empty place, carried west through Arabic books. Today's word.
Your line: nothing, as a number. Today, leave one place empty on purpose, five minutes with no task in it, and count it as part of the day. Day nine hundred eighteen.

919.title: Al-Kindi, the philosopher
919.hook: the philosopher of the Arabs, who wrote on optics, music and code-breaking
919.howItsDone: Muslim students of philosophy read al-Kindi as an early thinker who wrote philosophy in Arabic and held that reason and belief in one God could work together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, numbers from India: a small circle for the empty place, carried west in Arabic books. Your line was: nothing, as a number. Did you leave a place empty? Day nine hundred nineteen.

A letter arrives, and every word is scrambled. The letters have been swapped for other letters by a secret rule, and you don't know the rule. Where do you even start? A scholar in Baghdad wrote down an answer. Take a long ordinary text in the same language and count how often each letter appears. Then count the letters in the secret message. The sign that shows up most in the secret letter is probably standing in for the letter that shows up most in ordinary writing. Match them up, one by one, and the message begins to open. The man who wrote that method also wrote on light, on music, and on God. His name was al-Kindi.
screen: `A SCRAMBLED LETTER.` → `COUNT THE LETTERS.` → `THE MESSAGE OPENS.`

segments.voice: Yaqub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi worked in Baghdad in the age of the House of Wisdom, where Greek books were being turned into Arabic. Later writers gave him a title: the philosopher of the Arabs. He wrote philosophy in Arabic, using the new translations, asking the old Greek questions in the language of the Qur'an. His range is the first surprise. He wrote on optics, asking how rays travel and how we see. He wrote on music, on the strings of the oud and how notes fit together. He wrote on medicine, on the tides, on swords and perfumes, and on breaking codes, as in the hook. The second surprise is how he defends the whole project. Some people in his day were suspicious of learning that came from the Greeks. Al-Kindi answered, in his book on first philosophy, with an idea worth hearing slowly. He says we should not be ashamed to welcome the truth and take it in, wherever it comes from, even from distant peoples. The truth, he says, does not make the one who seeks it smaller. It honors him. And he wrote that philosophy at its highest is knowing the true One, the cause of all things. For al-Kindi, reason and faith in one God were meant to walk the same road. Muslim thinkers after him took different positions on how far philosophy should go, and that argument comes later in the path. Today, just meet one of its early voices.

segments.voice: The practice: learn one unusual fact. Before the bell, choose one small thing from today you didn't know, maybe that a philosopher broke codes by counting letters. Settle, and breathe. Hold the fact in mind. Turn it over. Where did it come from? Who first noticed it? Then let your mind rest on al-Kindi's idea: welcome the truth, wherever it comes from. If you pray, you can thank God for one thing you learned this week. If you don't, just be glad of it. The bell holds the time.

920.title: The hospitals
920.hook: hospitals treat all who come, rich or poor, with wards and music (historians)
920.howItsDone: Visiting the sick is a practice Muslims trace to the Prophet's teaching, and in Muslim history hospitals were often funded as waqf, a charitable endowment, so they could treat people who could not pay.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Kindi: codes, light, music, and truth welcomed from wherever it comes. Your line was: the philosopher of the arabs. What fact did you pick up? Day nine hundred twenty.

A traveler falls ill far from home. No family nearby, no money to speak of, no one who knows his name. That is a hard place to be. But historians describe, in the great cities of the Muslim world, a building where he could walk in the door. Separate wards for different illnesses. Physicians making rounds, students following them. A pharmacy. Water running through the courtyard. And in some of these houses, the historians say, musicians played for the patients, and storytellers sat with those who could not sleep. Nobody asked first whether he could pay. The building had a Persian name: bimaristan.
screen: `A TRAVELER FALLS ILL.` → `A DOOR THAT OPENS.` → `MUSIC IN THE WARDS.`

segments.voice: Bimaristan is usually explained as the place of the sick. The word came into Arabic from Persian, and in Cairo and Damascus, in Baghdad and beyond, it named a hospital. Three things made these houses work. First, the money. Historians describe them as paid for by waqf, an endowment: a ruler or a wealthy donor set aside shops, farms or rents forever, and their income kept the hospital open. Care was free because someone, long before, had given so it could be. Second, the order inside. Historians describe wards for fevers, for eye diseases, for surgery, for those whose minds were troubled. Physicians trained students at the bedside. Records were kept. Third, and most of all, the door: care for all who come. Men and women, rich and poor, locals and strangers. Muslims trace that door back to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, he tells his followers to feed the hungry, to visit the sick, and to free the captive. In another, he says that God has not sent down a disease without also sending down its cure. Visiting the sick was already a teaching of the Prophet. Looking for the cure was an act of hope. And the Qur'an, in a passage addressed to the Children of Israel, says that whoever saves one life, it is as if he had saved all humanity. Some have seen that verse put into stone in a hospital that turns no one away. Tomorrow, we meet one of the physicians who walked those wards.
screen: `BIMARISTAN: THE PLACE OF THE SICK.` · `PAID FOR BY WAQF.` · `WARDS, ROUNDS AND RECORDS.` · `VISIT THE SICK. SEEK THE CURE.` · then, large: `CARE FOR ALL WHO COME.`

segments.voice: The practice: give toward a hospital. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one hospital you know. Where you were born, or where someone you love was treated. Picture its door, and the people walking through it today, some of them frightened, some of them alone. Breathe for them. Then choose one small way to give: a donation, however small, to a hospital or a clinic that treats people who can't pay, or a visit to someone who is sick. If you pray, you can pray for the patients and the people caring for them. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.

921.title: Al-Razi the physician
921.hook: the physician who told smallpox from measles and ran Baghdad's hospital
921.howItsDone: Muslim physicians such as al-Razi kept careful case notes and wrote treatises on telling diseases apart, and his writings were studied by later doctors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bimaristan: an endowed hospital with its door open to rich and poor. Your line was: care for all who come. Who walked up to you, and did they get your full attention? Day nine hundred twenty-one.

Baghdad needs a new hospital, and someone has to choose where to put it. There is a story people tell about how it was done. The physician in charge had pieces of fresh meat hung up in different quarters of the city. Then he waited, and went around to look. Where the meat spoiled fastest, he reasoned, the air was worst. Where it stayed fresh longest, the sick would heal best. That is where the hospital should go. Whether it happened just that way, nobody can be sure; it comes from a later book of physicians' lives. But it fits what else is told about him. His name was Abu Bakr al-Razi.
screen: `WHERE SHOULD THE HOSPITAL GO?` → `MEAT HUNG ACROSS THE CITY.` → `WATCH WHERE IT SPOILS.`

segments.voice: Al-Razi means the man from Rayy, a city in Persia. He became a physician and led hospitals, in Rayy and in Baghdad, and his habit was simple and stubborn: look first. He kept notes on his patients, case after case, what they said, what he saw, what he gave them, and what happened next. After his death, his students gathered his notes into a huge book, al-Hawi, the comprehensive book, so that later doctors could learn from his bedside. One short work is on two diseases that came with fever and spots on the skin: smallpox and measles. Al-Razi watched closely and wrote down how they differed: how each began, how the rash came out, which signs warned of danger. Told apart, they could be treated apart. That is the whole method in a sentence. Observe, then treat. He also wrote that a doctor should not trust only the books. If what you see in a patient disagrees with what an old authority says, what is in front of you counts. And he did not write only for doctors with hospitals behind them. Al-Razi, the books say, wrote a little treatise for the poor: how to treat illness when there's no doctor and no money. Care for all who come, with your eyes open.
screen: `AL-RAZI, THE MAN FROM RAYY.` · `NOTES AT THE BEDSIDE.` · `SMALLPOX IS NOT MEASLES.` · `WHAT YOU SEE COUNTS.` · then, large: `OBSERVE, THEN TREAT.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a doctor. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a doctor or nurse who once looked at you closely, really looked, and saw what was wrong. Or one who cared for someone you love. Hold their face in mind. Breathe in. What did they notice that others missed? Breathe out. Then decide how you'll thank them, or someone like them: a message, a note, a word at your next appointment. If you pray, you can pray for the people who heal. If you don't, just hold your gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Al-Razi the physician. A doctor who led hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad, kept notes at the bedside, and told smallpox from measles by looking closely. Today's word.
Your line: observe, then treat. Today, before you try to fix someone's problem, ask one more question and listen to the whole answer. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

922.title: Ibn Sina
922.hook: the Canon of Medicine, a textbook in Europe and Asia for centuries
922.howItsDone: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was studied as a medical textbook, and in his own account of his life he describes turning to prayer in the mosque when a problem would not open.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Razi the physician: notes at the bedside, and smallpox told apart from measles. Your line was: observe, then treat. Did you ask one more question before fixing something? Day nine hundred twenty-two.

A young man is stuck. He has read a book of Greek philosophy over and over until he knows the words by heart, and still it makes no sense to him. He gives up on it. Then one afternoon, in the booksellers' market of Bukhara, a seller pushes a cheap little volume into his hands. He doesn't want it. The seller insists: the owner needs the money. He buys it, takes it home, and it turns out to be a short explanation of the very book that had defeated him. Suddenly, it opens. He says, in his own account, that he was so glad he went out and gave alms to the poor in thanks. The young man was Ibn Sina.
screen: `A BOOK THAT WON'T OPEN.` → `A CHEAP VOLUME IN THE MARKET.` → `ALMS IN THANKS.`

segments.voice: That story comes from Ibn Sina's own short account of his life, told to a student. In it he describes a boyhood of learning the Qur'an, then law, logic and mathematics, and then medicine, which he says he did not find hard. And he describes something else. When a problem defeated him, he would go to the mosque and pray, asking God to open what was closed, and then go back to work, sometimes into the night. Faith and study, in his telling, were part of one effort. His great medical book is called al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, the Canon of Medicine. Qanun means a rule, a standard. The Canon tried to gather what was known about the body into one ordered whole: how health is kept, how illness shows itself, which medicines do what, and how to treat each part of the body, head to foot. It made medicine something you could study in order, from first principles to particular cases. Historians describe the Canon being taught as a textbook for a long time, in Muslim lands and, in Latin translation, in the universities of Europe. One book, read by students who would never meet one another. And notice how the Canon defines medicine at its opening: the knowledge of the body in health and in illness, so that health can be kept, and restored when it is lost. Keeping comes before restoring. Whole sections deal with sleep, food, exercise, the air you breathe, the state of your mind. In the Canon, the body is cared for every day, not only rescued when it breaks.
screen: `A LIFE TOLD TO A STUDENT.` · `STUCK? GO TO THE MOSQUE AND PRAY.` · `QANUN: A RULE, A STANDARD.` · `KEEP HEALTH, THEN RESTORE IT.` · then, large: `THE CANON.`

segments.voice: The practice: take care of your body today. Settle, and breathe. Sit tall, feet on the floor. Move your attention slowly from your head down to your feet, the way the Canon moves through the body. Your head and eyes. Your neck and shoulders. Your chest as it breathes. Your stomach. Your legs. Your feet. Where is something asking for care? Choose one thing for today: water, a walk, an earlier night, a real meal. If you pray, you can thank God for the body you were given. If you don't, just thank it yourself. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Sina. A physician and philosopher who prayed when he was stuck and wrote the Canon of Medicine, one ordered book of the body. Today's word.
Your line: the canon. Today, keep one rule for your health, one small standard, and keep it all day. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

923.title: Al-Farabi, the second teacher
923.hook: the second teacher after Aristotle, on the virtuous city
923.howItsDone: Students of Islamic philosophy read al-Farabi's book on the virtuous city as a picture of a community that cooperates toward knowledge, goodness and happiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Sina: a cheap book from the market that opened a closed door, and the Canon, one ordered book of the body. Your line was: the canon. What rule for your health did you keep? Day nine hundred twenty-three.

That cheap little book Ibn Sina bought in the market had an author. He was a quiet scholar who, the stories say, cared little for money or fine clothes, and who could play music well enough to move a room. Later generations gave him a title with a weight to it. Aristotle, the great Greek, was called the first teacher. This man was called the second teacher. His name was Abu Nasr al-Farabi, and the question he kept coming back to is still asked in town councils and in group chats about where to live. What makes a city good?
screen: `THE AUTHOR OF THE CHEAP BOOK.` → `THE SECOND TEACHER.` → `WHAT MAKES A CITY GOOD?`

segments.voice: Al-Farabi wrote a book usually called the opinions of the people of the virtuous city. Al-madina al-fadila. His answer starts with a simple observation. Nobody can live well alone. People need one another for food, for safety, for learning. So they gather into villages, towns and cities. But gathering is not enough. What matters is what the city is for. Al-Farabi says the virtuous city is the one whose people cooperate to reach true happiness, which for him means a life of knowledge and goodness, in this world and beyond it. He pictures that city like a healthy body. Every part has its work, and every part helps the others, and the whole body lives well when each does its share. Then he describes other cities, the ones that miss the point. A city whose aim is only wealth. A city whose aim is only pleasure, or honor, or ruling over others. Their people may be busy and even rich, he says, but they have mistaken the road for the destination. And who should lead the good city? Al-Farabi pictures a ruler who is wise, truthful, just, and loves learning, a ruler like a heart that keeps the body alive. In al-Farabi's own account, this first ruler is both a philosopher, reaching the truth through reason, and a prophet, who brings it to people in words and images they can live by. Readers still argue over how he meant the two to fit. Either way, the test he sets is plain. The city's walls are not what makes it good. Its aim is.
screen: `NOBODY LIVES WELL ALONE.` · `A CITY AIMED AT HAPPINESS.` · `CITIES THAT MISS THE POINT.` · `A RULER LIKE A HEART.` · then, large: `THE VIRTUOUS CITY.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about a good city. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the place where you live: your street, your town, your building. Breathe in. Ask al-Farabi's question. What is this place for? Breathe out. Then picture it at its best. Who would be looked after who isn't now? What would people do together? Choose one part of the body you could be: the hands that help, the eyes that notice, the voice that speaks up. If you pray, you can pray for the place you live and the people in it. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Al-Farabi. The scholar called the second teacher, after Aristotle, who wrote that a city is good when its people work together toward true happiness. Today's word.
Your line: the virtuous city. Today, do one small thing that makes your street or building better for someone else, and notice what your city is for. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

924.title: Al-Biruni measures the earth
924.hook: who measured the earth's radius and wrote a careful study of India
924.howItsDone: Muslim scholars like al-Biruni studied geography and astronomy partly to find prayer times and the direction of Makkah, and his book on India is read as a careful account of another people's thought in its own terms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Farabi, the second teacher: a city is good when its people work together toward happiness. Your line was: the virtuous city. What did you do for your street? Day nine hundred twenty-four.

A man climbs a mountain with an instrument in his hands, in the land we now call Pakistan. He has already worked out how tall the mountain is. Now, at the top, he sights along the far horizon, where the plain meets the sky, and notes how far it dips below level. That's all. A height, and one small angle. From those two things, and some careful geometry, he works out the size of the whole earth. No ship sailing around it, no long journey. Just a mountain, a steady hand and patient math. His name was Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, and the mountain is only half his story.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN AND AN INSTRUMENT.` → `ONE SMALL ANGLE.` → `THE SIZE OF THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Al-Biruni wrote on astronomy, geography, minerals, calendars, and how far apart cities lay, partly so that people could find the direction of Makkah for prayer. The measuring on the mountain shows his habit. Check the height. Check the angle. Check the math. The Qur'an says that God created everything by measure, and al-Biruni measured as if that were true of every stone and star. But today's deeper lesson is his other great book. He spent long stretches in India, learned Sanskrit, read the Indian sciences and scriptures in their own language, and talked with Indian scholars. Then he wrote a book about India, its beliefs, its philosophy, its astronomy, its customs and its calendar. Listen to how it begins. In his opening, al-Biruni says the book is not a book of argument. He will set out what the Hindus themselves say, in their own words, as faithfully as he can, and where their thinkers resemble the Greeks, he will show that too. He complains about earlier writers who reported on other peoples from hearsay, copying mistakes and adding insults. He refuses to do that. Of course al-Biruni was a Muslim, and his book does not hide it. But he measured another people's thought the way he measured a mountain. Carefully. Without bending the numbers. That is a hard thing to do with a mountain. It's harder still with a neighbor's faith.

segments.voice: The practice: study another culture respectfully. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one tradition or culture you know only from the outside, maybe from headlines or from a friend. Breathe in. What do you think you know about it? Breathe out. Now ask al-Biruni's question: did I learn that from them, in their own words, or from hearsay? Choose one thing you'll read or ask, from someone inside that tradition, this week. If you pray, you can ask God for a fair mind. If you don't, just hold the question open. The bell holds the time.
Al-Biruni measures the earth. A scholar who found the size of the earth from a mountaintop, and wrote about India from its own books, in its own words. Today's word.

Your line: measure carefully. This week we met numbers from India, a philosopher, a hospital, two physicians, a second teacher and a measurer. Today, before you describe anyone else's beliefs, check the measure. Day nine hundred twenty-four.
